catalog_quote: A note on pronunciation: both Awyu and Yaqay have a predominance of stress on the final syllable of a word. Thus place names are pronounced Ketá, Kotúp, Nohón, Bagarám, Wanggaté, Kogó, and Rayám, among others. Also, the “q” in Yaqay and the “gh” in Aghu represent voiced velar fricatives.

Thus place names are pronounced Ketá, Kotúp, Nohón, Bagarám, Wanggaté, Kogó, and Rayám, among others. Also, the “q” in Yaqay and the “gh” in Aghu represent voiced velar fricatives.
new_statements.citation: Kriens, Ronald & Randy Lebold. 2010. Report on the Wildeman River Survey in Papua, Indonesia. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2010-010. Dallas: SIL International.
new_statements.locator: p. 5, section 2 'Background information' (paragraph 'A note on pronunciation')
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check:, printed p. 5 (= p. 5), section 2 'BACKGROUND INFORMATION', last paragraph: 'A note on pronunciation: both Awyu and Yaqay have a predominance of stress on the final syllable of a word. Thus place names are pronounced Ketá, Kotúp, Nohón, Bagarám, Wanggaté, Kogó, and Rayám, among others. Also, the "q" in Yaqay and the "gh" in Aghu represent voiced velar fricatives.' -- verbatim as reported (extracted text of the copy consulted). Surrounding section read: sec. 1 'Previous work' names Drabbe 1954 as the Yaqay grammar; sec. 2 identifies the Yaqay [jaq] people around Kepi, bordering Awyu to the west, language related to Warkay-Bipim [bgv]; villages surveyed Kotup, Wanggate, Kogo, Ray…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress predominantly falls on the final syllable of the word (stated as a tendency, illustrated with place names); no fuller analysis given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said (appendix IPA wordlists occasionally mark secondary stress with ˌ but without discussion).
new_statements.exceptions: None named; the wording 'predominance' implies non-final cases exist, and the appendix wordlists show some Yaqay items transcribed with non-final stress (e.g. ˈteŋɣit͡s 'stone' at Kotup vs tiŋˈgi at Kogo).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, based on survey-team impressions and citation-form place names/wordlist elicitation (North Yakhai villages Kogo, Kotup, Rayam, Wairu, Wanggate, Obaa subdistrict); this is a sociolinguistic survey report, not a phonological analysis. The only dedicated phonology (Kainakainu et al. 1998, South Yakhai) is silent on stress; Drabbe 1954 (Jaqaj grammar, MBA 11) was not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted note (Kriens & Lebold 2010) concerns Yaqay as surveyed in the Obaa subdistrict villages Kogo, Kotup, Rayam, Wairu, Wanggate, i.e. North Yakhai in Usher's terms (Drabbe's 'Jaqàj' of the Mapi/Qobamarao is also North Yakhai). The 1998 Indonesian phonology 'Fonologi Bahasa Yakhai' (silent on stress) describes South Yakhai (Kec. Obaa east / Nambioman Bapai). All fall under glottocode yaqa1246 (no Glottolog dialect codes). Note the survey authors treat 'Yaqay' as possibly two closely related languages.

sources.note: No Jaqaj stress rule. Introduction (p. xx-xxii): 'The weak point in the material of Father Drabbe is the lack of a phonetic transcription'.. 'a bold lettertype indicates stress. sources.note: A one-page structural sketch after Drabbe 1954 gives the phoneme inventory (4 voiceless stops, 3 voiced stops, 3 nasals, flap, 2 semivowels, 7 vowels) and one prosodic sentence: Drabbe describes Yaqay stress as 'a kind of pitch accent' and does not say whether it is phonemic. No tone inventory, no accent-placement rule; the only accessible characterisation of Yaqay word prosody as pitch-based, second-hand from the unobtained Drabbe 1954 pp. 73-75.
